newsitem.title: USA: Amnesty calls for halt in U.S. aid to Colombia.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty calls for halt in U.S. aid to Colombia.

text.p: Amnesty International urged the United States on Tuesday to suspend arms sales and anti-drugs aid to Colombia, whose military it accused of killing civilians with U.S.-supplied weapons.

Officials of the London-based human rights group said they had obtained leaked documents indicating that Colombian army units involved in atrocities were using arms and military equipment acquired from or granted by the United States.

"Because of this new information, provided by a U.S. official deeply troubled by U.S. policy in Colombia, we are today calling for the immediate suspension of U.S. military assistance to Colombia," William Schulz, Amnesty International's executive director in Washington, said.

Schulz told a news conference his group was seeking a halt to a shipment of $40 million in military aid offered to Colombia by President Bill Clinton in September, as well as the sale of "Black Hawk" helicopters.

He said such sales and all military aid to Colombia should be delayed until Washington comes up with a plan to prevent more abuses involving U.S.-supplied equipment and discloses past recipients of its assistance.

Amnesty says more than 20,000 people have been killed in Colombia since 1986 due not to drug-related violence but to politically motivated assassinations and massacres. "Most of these deaths have been the responsibility of the military and its paramilitary allies and most of the victims have been innocent civilians," Schulz said.

Amnesty made similar charges, which the U.S. State Department denied, in 1994. It based its fresh charges on three documents it obtained from an American investigative reporter who in turn got them from a U.S. official, Amnesty Latin America specialist Carlos Salinas said.
The reporter, freelance Frank Smyth of Washington, DC, declined to say where he had obtained the documents.

One of them was a 1994 report drafted by a U.S. army colonel on the U.S. Southern Command's "vulnerability" in light of human rights violations in Colombia. Addressed to the regional commander, Gen. Barry McCaffrey, who is now Clinton's anti-drug czar, it concluded that their legal and political liability was "slight."

Another document was a list of suspect Colombian military units that Amnesty provided to the State Department in 1994. This copy had handwritten annotations that appeared to be the locations of various brigades and battalions.

The third document, which had no letterhead, carried the title "Equipment Acquired Through U.S. Grants." The four-page list included all but one of the units named in Amnesty's letter to the State Deparment, with details of equipment such as military vehicles, machineguns, grenades, mines and ammunition obtained by each.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns declined to comment on the leaked documents but said the U.S. government would look into the points raised by Amnesty International.
"We are very clear that the military assistance that we provide to Colombia must be used for the purposes intended -- counter-narcotics," Burns told reporters.
